question: What escalation rule should govern when an agent must get owner approval before acting, versus proceeding autonomously, via consensus-plus-notify, or via two independent reviews -- and how should the rule itself, and owner intent behind any of it, ever be verified?
options: Adopt the refined, eight-point escalation rule below in full: owner-approve-first for five named categories (irreversible/speaks-for-owner effects, authority changes, standing-setting changes, unresolved value disagreements, and owner-reserved areas), a new consensus-plus-notify path for single-revert-restorable changes, two independent reviews (with blind verdicts, a fresh final reviewer, and model-diversity recording for governance/security/gate work) for everything else, mechanical tier assignment that a reviewer may only raise, owner decisions sourced only from agent-unwritable channels, and this rule's own amendment path locked to owner ratification.

Keep operating under the original, less detailed decision-tier rule at #1187 comment 5800142871 alone, without ratifying the refinements above (no consensus-plus-notify path, no blind-verdict/fresh-reviewer/model-diversity requirements, no channel-sourcing rule for owner decisions, no explicit amendment-lock on the rule itself).
recommendation: Option 1 (adopt the refined rule in full) -- the coordinator's own recommendation when presenting it for ratification: "Final rule for your ratification … Recommendation: ratify."
decision:
The coordinator presented this rule for ratification in the coordinator chat on 2026-09-23 at approximately 14:35 PDT ("Final rule for your ratification … Recommendation: ratify"), and the owner replied "go". The ratified rule, reproduced here in full and without addition or weakening (the same text also appears in docs/HITL.md's "Escalation rule" section, which is the living, applied copy; this record is the durable, append-only source of truth for what was actually ratified):

1. Owner-approve-first (blocking) applies when any of these hold:
   (a) irreversible effects, or public text that speaks for or commits the owner. That means publish, delete, money, credentials, workflow secrets or permissions, announcements, commitments to third parties, release notes, and messages to people. Routine safety-gated PR and issue comments by agents are NOT this category.
   (b) authority changes: who decides what, a gate switching to enforce, tier definitions, the model allowlist, this rule. Judge them on the cumulative change since the owner last approved that gate. An enforce ask must include measured report-only results (false positives and misses).
   (c) changes to standing owner settings: cadence, thresholds, risk appetite, budgets. One-off choices inside an existing setting belong to the agents.
   (d) value disagreements, or no convergence after 3 rounds. For severity disagreements, take the stricter view and fix; don't escalate.
   (e) anything the owner has reserved. The owner can also explicitly release an area back to the agents.
   Asks carry a recommendation, a default and a deadline, and are batched to the Friday cut-off unless urgent. Before asking, apply the ask-quality test: what would the agents do differently if the owner said no?
2. Consensus + notify: only for changes a single revert fully restores, with nothing external happening in between. Two reviews, then a decision-log entry. The digest holds at most 5 items, ranked by risk, each with its revert. If the owner vetoes nothing for 8 weeks, shrink the notify scope.
3. Two independent reviews for everything else. For governance, security and gate work: both reviewers strong-reasoning class, verdicts formed blind (before reading the other's), and a fresh final reviewer with no history on the PR. Record model diversity.
4. Autonomous: tier-0 paths, logged.
5. Tier assignment is mechanical, by path rules. A reviewer may raise a tier, never lower it. When in doubt, the higher tier applies. The coordinator doesn't pick its own tier.
6. Owner decisions are recorded only from channels agents can't write to: owner chat now, commits signed with an owner-only hardware key later. A GitHub comment under the shared identity is never proof of owner intent. Chat-sourced records say "channel: owner-chat, not independently verifiable".
7. Changing this rule: agents propose, only the owner ratifies (chat, or later a signed commit). The rule file and the deny hook are write-protected from agents in the deny hook. Consensus + notify NEVER applies to changes to this rule. Interpretations and classification precedents count as rule changes.
8. Owner pushback changes a tier only through an explicit reservation or release. Agents defend their classification with reasons.

Classified tier-2 here under the rule's own item 1(b) ("authority changes: … this rule") and item 7 ("Consensus + notify NEVER applies to changes to this rule") -- this record documents the rule's own adoption, so it is bound by the rule's strictest self-referential category from the moment it exists.
notes: channel: owner-chat, not independently verifiable (per the rule's own item 6, applied reflexively to its own ratification record). No `reviews[]` entries: this was a business/priority ratification the owner made directly in chat after the coordinator's own recommendation, not a prior agent recommendation with a citable, durable link an entry here could point to (docs/contracts/decision-record.json's own note: `reviews` may be empty for a `decidedBy: "owner"` record made without a prior agent recommendation). This record's `decision` field embeds the full ratified rule text verbatim so it survives as a self-contained artifact even if docs/HITL.md's own prose is later edited, reworded, or reorganized -- docs/HITL.md's "Escalation rule" section is the living, applied copy meant for day-to-day reading, but THIS record is the one that could resolve a dispute about what was actually ratified. Nothing in this record adds to or weakens the rule as ratified; item 7's own text ("Interpretations and classification precedents count as rule changes") is taken seriously here -- this record deliberately does not interpret, elaborate, or apply the rule to any specific case, only states what was ratified. governance/review-tiers.json's own tier-2 classification of `governance/decisions/**`-adjacent enforcement-surface files, and of this file's own sibling `docs/contracts/decision-record.json` and `scripts/check-decision-records.mjs` (both extended alongside this record to carry a `channel` field), means the pull request that adds this record is itself tier-2 by the CODE's existing classification too, independent of this record's own `tier` field -- the two are consistent, not coincidentally.
